atoms.text:
In this level, you will read about three key moments in Britain's history of racism, anti-immigrant sentiment and hate crime:

• the 1958 Notting Hill Race Riots
• the rise of the anti-immigrant movement in the 1970s
• the 2005 London bombings.

Trigger warning: the texts mention racist violence, terrorism and discrimination.

atoms.b:
1958: Notting Hill Race Riots and Resistance

((++Racist_attacks))
In the late summer of 1958, violent mobs (many of them members of far-right groups) attacked the homes of West Indian residents in the Notting Hill district of London over several nights.

((A_hostile_welcome))
The riots exposed the deep racial hostility that many Caribbean migrants had faced since their arrival, despite having been actively recruited by the British government.

((Resistance --Assimilation))
Rather than retreating, the community responded defiantly. Trinidadian activist and journalist Claudia Jones organised an indoor Caribbean carnival the following year, which eventually grew into a powerful symbol of Black British culture and resilience.

The 1970s: The Rise of the Anti-Immigration Movement

The 1970s saw a sharp rise in organised ((++opposition --consent)) to immigration in Britain. The National Front, a ((++far-right --far-left)) political party, marched through areas with large immigrant populations, distributing racist propaganda. Racially motivated attacks on South Asian and Caribbean communities ((++increased --decreased)) significantly.

In 1968, Conservative politician Enoch Powell had already ((++worsened --cancelled)) tensions with a speech, in which he warned of the consequences of continued immigration. Though Powell was dismissed from the shadow cabinet, his speech gave mainstream respectability to ((++anti-immigrant --pro-immigrant)) sentiment, and its effects were felt throughout the decade.

atoms.text:
2005: The London Bombings

On the morning of 7 July 2005, four suicide bombers detonated explosives on three Underground trains and a bus in central London, killing 52 people and injuring hundreds more. The four bombers were British citizens, three of them born and raised in Leeds to Pakistani immigrant families. The attacks provoked intense national debate about integration, identity and radicalisation and led to a significant increase in anti-Muslim hate crimes. At the same time, many Muslim community leaders and organisations publicly condemned the bombings, and voices across the political spectrum warned against blaming an entire community for the actions of a few.
